definition: A token is a small chunk of text — roughly four characters in English — that an AI model reads and writes. The model never sees whole words or sentences the way you do; it sees a stream of tokens. "Hello" is one token, "unbelievable" is three.

edges.label: too many →
edges.note: Pile up enough tokens — especially output tokens — and you get token burn.

example.body: The sentence "Can you summarize this 40-page contract?" is about 12 tokens going in — cheap. The 3,000-token summary coming back is where the cost lives. Output tokens almost always cost more than input tokens, which is why long answers are the expensive part.
example.title: Counting the cost of a sentence

footnotes.body: Most models use subword tokenization (e.g. byte-pair encoding). The same text can be a different number of tokens on different models. Pricing is typically quoted per million tokens, split into input and output rates — output is usually priced higher.
footnotes.label: For the technical reader

name: Token
tagline: The small chunks of text an AI reads and writes — and the unit everything is billed in.
whyItMatters: Tokens are the currency of AI. How much a request costs, how long it takes, and how much the model can remember at once are all measured in tokens. Once you start thinking in tokens, surprise bills and slow answers start making sense.
